MENINGITIS 
By: Colum Bowyer, Charlotte Price, Tairice Cash, Cary Pang, Christelle 
Louis, Coda Collins, Angelina Fordjour, Matthew Cocco

RISK FACTORS           PREVENTION
• Age-related risks: newborns are at higher risk for Group 
B streptococcus; children and adults commonly develop 
meningitis from Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria 
meningitidis; older adults have increased risk for 
pneumococcal disease
• Close living conditions such as college dorms or 
military barracks.
• Recent respiratory or ear infections
• Head trauma
• Travel
• Immune deficiency or immunocompromised states such as 
HIV or cancer
• For viral meningitis, common causes include enteroviruses, 
herpesviruses, influenza, mumps, and arboviruses like West 
Nile virus and Zika
• Vaccination is the best prevention for common bacterial 
causes. Encourage vaccination against Haemophilus influenzae 
type b (Hib) and Streptococcus pneumoniae in children and 
adults at risk
• The two main types of meningococcal vaccines recommended for 
adolescents are the MenACWY (Meningococcal Conjugate) vaccine 
and the MenB (Serogroup B) vaccine.  
• Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of someone with meningococcal 
meningitis:
  - Rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone
      - Start within 24 hours after exposure for best effectiveness
Nursing considerations: 
• Place the patient in a private room on droplet precautions at 
the first suspicion of bacterial meningitis (before lab 
confirmation).
• Give prescribed broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., 
ceftriaxone, vancomycin) as soon as possible. Do not delay.
• Elevate the head of the bed to 30 degrees and keep the head 
and neck in a neutral, midline position to promote venous 
drainage and lower intracranial pressure (ICP).

HEALTH 
PROMOTION/EARLY 
DETECTION 
• Prevention: Vaccinate (meningococcal at 11–12, booster at 16; Hib; pneumococcal); finish full antibiotic courses.
• Adult Presentation: Fever, severe headache, photophobia, nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig/Brudzinski signs, and altered mental status (key 
in older adults).
• Pediatric Presentation: Non-specific in infants (lethargy, poor feeding, late nuchal rigidity); fever + seizure = assumed meningitis until 
proven otherwise.
• Diagnosis: Rapid blood/CSF cultures and Gram stain.
• Safety Precaution: CT before lumbar puncture if immunocompromised, altered consciousness, papilledema, or new seizures (prevents 
brain herniation).
• Education: Teach early recognition of symptoms, worsening consciousness, and increased ICP signs.

CLINICAL 
MANIFESTATION
S 
Common / Initial
• Persistent high-grade fever and 
chills
• Severe headache  (steady or 
throbbing)
• Nuchal rigidity (stiff, painful 
neck)
• Photophobia (light sensitivity)
• Nausea & vomiting
• Tachycardia
Neurologic 
Manifestations
• Confusion / altered mental 
status
• Seizures
• Lethargy / coma / 
unresponsiveness
• Increased intracranial pressure 
(ICP)
• Positive Kernig & Brudzinski 
signs
Meningococcal 
Meningitis
• Petechial / purpuric rash
• Large areas of ecchymosis
Acute fulminant 
infection
• Abrupt high fever
• Shock 
• Disseminated intravascular 
coagulation (DIC)

DX TESTS (NURSING 
RESPONSIBILITIES) 
• Lumbar puncture – collect CSF for lab analysis
 - NB: CT scan before lumbar puncture
 - informed consent
 - assistance during procedure
 - post-lumbar puncture headache
• Blood culture and Gram staining

MEDICATION MANAGEMENT & NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES
Neurologic support: 
•  Monitor for increasing ICP
o  (Cushing's triad) 
• Monitor level of consciousness
• Monitor Pupillary response 
Blood pressure:
• Monitored with an arterial line for  early signs of 
shock.
• Oral or IV Fluid replacement
Temperature regulation:
• Fever can increase the workload of the heart 
and raise cerebral metabolism. 
• Apply antipyretics, cooling blankets if feverish
Respiratory support: 
• Monitor pulse ox and arterial blood gas
• Initiate mechanical ventilation if necessary 
Prevent complications:
• Prevent injury from seizure activity
• Prevent pressure injuries from immobility. 
• Daily weight if SIADH suspected
Regular vital signs and neuro 
checks 
• Every 15-30 minutes during the first 2 
hours of acute phase
• Every 2-4 hours afterwards
Isolation precaution
• Droplet precautions for bacterial 
meningitis until 24 hours after antibiotic 
therapy
• Standard precautions for viral 
meningitis
For all meningitis patients 
Medication Management  Nursing considerations
Penicillin G(IV)
• Check patient for allergies to penicillin, and monitor for signs of 
anaphylaxis
• Monitor bowel function for signs of CDAD(diarrhea, cramping)
Cephalosporin (e.g. ceftriaxone, cefotaxime)
• Educate patient to avoid alcohol
• Monitor renal function (BUN, creatinine) and adjust dose if 
necessary.
• Educate patient to complete the  full abx course
• Monitor for rash – could be a sign of SJS
Dexamethosone
• Monitor fluid and electrolyte balance (I+O, daily weight). 
• Monitor blood sugar levels for hyperglycemia, especially with 
diabetes

PATIENT EDUCATION 
• Recognize warning signs requiring immediate medical attention: fever, severe headache, stiff neck, confusion, 
seizures, or petechial rash
•Complete the full course of prescribed antibiotics 
• Follow droplet precautions during the first 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy for meningococcal 
meningitis; close contacts may require prophylactic antibiotics
• Practice good hand hygiene; avoid sharing drinks, utensils, or personal items
• Stay up to date with recommended meningococcal, pneumococcal, and Hib vaccinations
• Attend follow-up appointments and report hearing loss, memory changes, balance problems, or other 
neurologic changes

DISCHARGE PLANNING & 
HOMECARE 
•  Rest quietly in dim rooms and increase activity slowly
• Return to school, work and driving only when provider has cleared 
• Review medications list, doses, and schedule. Arrange IV antibiotics if ordered by the provider 
• Use acetaminophen for fever as directed. Ask provider before using NSAIDs
• Arrange for OT, PT, or home health nursing if needed
• Educate patient on follow-up appointments such as audiological testing, before discharge or within 
four weeks after discharge
